title: Frontend Composition
subject: main
summary: Composition rules exist so that every page in the product reads the same way and no page can invent its own authorization. A developer opening any page finds…

axioms.text: The route layer translates and guards. It turns the URL into plain props, picks the shell, and runs the route guards — nothing else.
sub: No page data fetching, no permission-derived rendering, no injected callbacks.
The guards are the session check and the obligations gate ([[unmet-requirements|Unmet Requirements]]); their only outcomes are pass, login, or the resolve flow.

axioms.text: A page fetches its own data and renders what the backend returned.
sub: It reads what it needs from props and from context, and owns its loading and error states.
Empty data renders an empty state. It is never a redirect.

axioms.text: The frontend never decides authorization. The backend returns capability flags and the page reads them.
sub: No client-side role checks, no visibility computed from config, no redirect based on permission state.
Two permitted redirects: unauthenticated → login, and unmet obligations → the resolve flow ([[unmet-requirements|Unmet Requirements]]). A restricted page renders empty — restriction never redirects.

axioms.text: There is one page-entry pattern, and every page is an instance of it.
sub: A login page is the same shape with the capability step switched off; a members list is the same shape with every step on. The structure never changes.

axioms.text: A [[slice]] consumes app capabilities through injected adapters, never by importing the app.
sub: Router, toast, query client — plus the config the slice builds its own API client from. The direction is always app provides → slice consumes.

purpose.intro: Composition rules exist so that every page in the product reads the same way and no page can invent its own authorization. A developer opening any page finds data fetched in the same place, capability flags read from the same source, and loading and error handled with the same primitives — whichever [[slice]] owns it.
points: **One shape:** the route translates, the page fetches and renders, the shared primitives handle the states in between.
**One authority:** what a user may see and do comes from the backend, in the response, every time.
purpose.note: Where this code lives and who may import it is not here — that is [[scaffolding-and-import-boundaries|Scaffolding & Import Boundaries]]. This doc is only about what happens inside a page.

reference.topic: Structure comes from the layouts library
reference.statement: Every structural region on screen is a `@libs/web-layouts` component. Nobody hand-rolls structure.

claims.text: The app picks the [[shell]] per route — `shell-side-nav`, `shell-top-nav` or `shell-none`. Shell primitives are app-level only.

Auth pages fill the `AuthPage` [[composition]]; other [[slice]] pages render into app-level section layouts (`PageFrame`, `SettingsLayout`) that assemble primitives. A page never builds a shell and never writes structural CSS.
A [[page]] fills the whole `page` region; a [[sub-page]] fills `main` inside a [[section]], which owns `page-header` and `left-sidebar`.

reference.statement: Every page enters the same way. The route layer above it translates and wraps; the page itself fetches and renders; the shared primitives below it carry the states. Naming the three layers is what stops data fetching drifting up into routes and authorization drifting down into pages.

claims.text: The route layer translates URL params and search params into plain props, chooses the shell that wraps the page, and runs the route guards. That is all it does.
The page reads its props and its context, calls the backend, reads capability flags from the response, handles its own loading and error states, and renders the result.
Loading skeletons, error boundaries, dialogs and layout primitives come from the shared UI [[library|libraries]] — a page never rolls its own.
By the time any page renders, the session is already hydrated on the provider tree. No page resolves it.

imagesAndDiagrams.title: One page, three layers
imagesAndDiagrams.value:
ROUTE LAYER                                            owned by the app
│  URL params · search params  →  plain props
│  picks the shell · runs the guards (session, obligations gate)
│  no page fetching · no permission-derived rendering · no callbacks
▼
PAGE COMPONENT                       owned by whoever owns the page
│  1. receives plain props
│  2. reads context (api client, auth, config, session)
│  3. calls the backend over HTTP, fetches its own data
│  4. reads capability flags from the response — the backend is the authority
│  5. handles its own loading and error states
│  6. renders what came back. empty data → empty state, never a redirect
▼
SHARED UI PRIMITIVES                                   shared libraries
   skeletons · error boundaries · dialogs · layout primitives

reference.statement: Who may render a menu depends on who owns the pages behind it. Three cases, and the third is the one that gets built wrong.

claims.text: A slice may render navigation to its own pages when clicking changes the URL. It contributed those routes and assumes the app mounted them; the app's router does the rest.
A slice may render navigation that changes only its own local state — a wizard's steps, a tab that swaps content. No URL, no app involvement.
A menu whose targets span more than one owner cannot be slice-owned. The app renders it, and the slices contribute metadata into it.

reference.statement: Sheets and modals split three ways: the primitive, the orchestration, and the content shown inside. Only the middle one is contested.

claims.text: Overlay primitives — sheet, dialog, modal — live in the shared UI libraries. The slice-specific content inside belongs to the slice showing it.
An overlay that can stack, or that needs shell-level coordination, goes through the app's overlay controller: one host, one stack, one z-index system.
A self-contained dialog or confirm that never stacks may stay slice-local, built from the shared primitives.

reference.statement: Four kinds of state, four homes. Choosing by habit rather than by kind is what produces a global store nobody can reason about.

claims.text: Server state lives in the query cache — it is a cache of the backend, never a copy to be edited.
Genuinely global UI state (sidebar open, theme) lives in a small global store, and stays small.
Filters, pagination and sorting live in the URL, so a page is shareable and reloadable.
